Tables

2026-10-01

tables.Rmd

Tables

Synapse Tables enable storage of tabular data in Synapse in a form that can be queried using a SQL-like query language.

A table has a schema and holds a set of rows conforming to that schema. A schema defines a series of Columns of the following types: STRING, DOUBLE, INTEGER, BOOLEAN, DATE, ENTITYID, FILEHANDLEID, LINK, LARGETEXT, MEDIUMTEXT, USERID, SUBMISSIONID, EVALUATIONID, JSON, STRING_LIST, INTEGER_LIST, BOOLEAN_LIST, DATE_LIST, ENTITYID_LIST, USERID_LIST.

Tutorial purpose

In this vignette you will:

  1. Create a Table and load it with data
  2. Query your Table
  3. Update your Table
  4. Change Table structure
  5. Delete Table rows and Tables
  6. Work with dates and datetimes

Prerequisites

  1. Make sure that you have completed the Project tutorial.
  2. The tutorial assumes you have data in a dataframe and/or CSV you want to query in a SQL like interface in Synapse

1. Creating a table

Initial setup 

library(synapser)
## 
## TERMS OF USE NOTICE:
##   When using Synapse, remember that the terms and conditions of use require that you:
##   1) Attribute data contributors when discussing these data or results from these data.
##   2) Not discriminate, identify, or recontact individuals or groups represented by the data.
##   3) Use and contribute only data de-identified to HIPAA standards.
##   4) Redistribute data only under these same terms of use.
synLogin()
## Welcome, Dan Lu!
## NULL

project = Project(
  name = paste0(
    "My uniquely named project about Alzheimer's Disease ",
    paste(sample(c(letters, LETTERS, 0:9), 8, replace = TRUE), collapse = "")
  )
) |> synStore()
cat("Created project:", project$id, "\n")
## Created project: syn77515198

Example data

First, let’s load some data. Let’s say we had a file, genes.csv:

Name Chromosome Start End Strand TranscriptionFactor
foo 1 12345 12600 + False
arg 2 20001 20200 + False
zap 2 30033 30999 - False
bah 1 40444 41444 - False
bnk 1 51234 54567 + True
xyz 1 61234 68686 + False 
genes_csv = tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
writeLines(
  c(
    "Name,Chromosome,Start,End,Strand,TranscriptionFactor",
    "foo,1,12345,12600,+,False",
    "arg,2,20001,20200,+,False",
    "zap,2,30033,30999,-,False",
    "bah,1,40444,41444,-,False",
    "bnk,1,51234,54567,+,True",
    "xyz,1,61234,68686,+,False"
  ),
  genes_csv
)

Loading data

  • Creating a table from a CSV without specifying initial columns. In older versions of synapser, this was implemented using synBuildTable().
table = Table(
  name = "My Favorite Genes_no_initial_columns",
  parent_id = project$id
) |> synStore()

table |> synStoreRows(
  values = genes_csv,
  schema_storage_strategy = "INFER_FROM_DATA"
)
## NULL

synStoreRows() accepts data from several sources:

  • A string holding the path to a CSV file. If the schema_storage_strategy is set to NULL the data will be uploaded as is. If schema_storage_strategy is set to INFER_FROM_DATA, the code makes assumptions about the format of the columns in the CSV.

  • A named list where each name is a column name and each value is one or more values.

  • An R data frame.

  • Creating a table from a CSV with specified columns

columns = list(
  Column(name = "Name", column_type = "STRING", maximum_size = 20),
  Column(name = "Chromosome", column_type = "STRING", maximum_size = 20),
  Column(name = "Start", column_type = "INTEGER"),
  Column(name = "End", column_type = "INTEGER"),
  Column(name = "Strand", column_type = "STRING", enum_values = list("+", "-"), maximum_size = 1),
  Column(name = "TranscriptionFactor", column_type = "BOOLEAN")
)
table = Table(
  name = "My Favorite Genes_with_columns",
  columns = columns,
  parent_id = project$id
) |> synStore()
table |> synStoreRows(values = genes_csv)
## NULL
  • Creating a table from a data frame
genes = tibble::tibble(
  Name = c("foo", "arg", "zap", "bah", "bnk", "xyz"),
  Chromosome = c("1", "2", "2", "1", "1", "1"),
  Start = c(12345L, 20001L, 30033L, 40444L, 51234L, 61234L),
  End = c(12600L, 20200L, 30999L, 41444L, 54567L, 68686L),
  Strand = c("+", "+", "-", "-", "+", "+"),
  TranscriptionFactor = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

table = Table(
  name = "My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe",
  parent_id = project$id
) |> synStore()
table |> synStoreRows(values = genes, schema_storage_strategy = "INFER_FROM_DATA")
## [syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe:Column_Name (Add)]: Column(id=None, name='Name', column_type=STRING, facet_type=None, default_value=None, maximum_size=50, maximum_list_length=None, enum_values=None, json_sub_columns=None)[syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe:Column_Chromosome (Add)]: Column(id=None, name='Chromosome', column_type=STRING, facet_type=None, default_value=None, maximum_size=50, maximum_list_length=None, enum_values=None, json_sub_columns=None)[syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe:Column_Start (Add)]: Column(id=None, name='Start', column_type=INTEGER, facet_type=None, default_value=None, maximum_size=None, maximum_list_length=None, enum_values=None, json_sub_columns=None)[syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe:Column_End (Add)]: Column(id=None, name='End', column_type=INTEGER, facet_type=None, default_value=None, maximum_size=None, maximum_list_length=None, enum_values=None, json_sub_columns=None)[syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe:Column_Strand (Add)]: Column(id=None, name='Strand', column_type=STRING, facet_type=None, default_value=None, maximum_size=50, maximum_list_length=None, enum_values=None, json_sub_columns=None)[syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe:Column_TranscriptionFactor (Add)]: Column(id=None, name='TranscriptionFactor', column_type=BOOLEAN, facet_type=None, default_value=None, maximum_size=None, maximum_list_length=None, enum_values=None, json_sub_columns=None)[syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe]: (Column Order): ['Name', 'Chromosome', 'Start', 'End', 'Strand', 'TranscriptionFactor'][syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe]: Found 1 chunks to upload into table
## NULL

2. Querying for data

The query language is quite similar to SQL select statements, except that joins are not supported. The documentation for the Synapse API has lots of query examples. Let’s try to query:

results = synQuery(sprintf("SELECT * FROM %s WHERE Chromosome = '1' AND Start < 41000 AND \"End\" > 20000", table$id))
## [syn77792773]: Downloaded to /Users/danlu/.synapseCache/475/177767475/SYNAPSE_TABLE_QUERY_177767475.csv
results
##   ROW_ID ROW_VERSION Name Chromosome Start   End Strand TranscriptionFactor
## 1      4           1  bah          1 40444 41444      -               FALSE

The synQuery() will always be returned as a data frame unless you specify a download_location in which case the results will be downloaded to that location. There are a number of arguments that you may pass to this function depending on if you are getting the results back as a DataFrame or downloading the results to a file.

3. Changing Data

Once the schema is settled, changes come in two flavors: appending new rows and updating existing ones. One other piece of information required for making changes to tables is the etag, which is used by the Synapse server to prevent concurrent users from making conflicting changes through a technique called optimistic concurrency. This comes as a result of running synQuery. In the example above, you could see the etag by running results$etag - but you should never have to use it directly. In case of a conflict, your update may be rejected. You then have to do another query and try your update again.

Appending new rows

Appending new rows is fairly straightforward. To continue the previous example, we might add some new genes from another file. Lets take this new data in more_genes.csv.

The more_genes.csv: | Name | Chromosome | Start | End | Strand | TranscriptionFactor | |——|————|——–|——–|——–|———————| | Qux1 | 4 | 201001 | 202001 | + | False | | Qux2 | 4 | 203001 | 204001 | + | False |

  • Using a CSV
more_genes_csv = tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
writeLines(
  c(
    "Name,Chromosome,Start,End,Strand,TranscriptionFactor",
    "Qux1,4,201001,202001,+,False",
    "Qux2,4,203001,204001,+,False"
  ),
  more_genes_csv
)

table = Table(
  name = "My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe",
  parent_id = project$id
) |> synGet()
table |> synStoreRows(values = more_genes_csv)
## NULL
  • Using a data frame If a column is not given, NA values are added automatically.
moreGenes = tibble::tibble(
  Name = c("Qux3", "Qux4"),
  Chromosome = c("4", "4"),
  Start = c(201001L, 203001L),
  End = c(202001L, 204001L),
  Strand = c("+", "+"),
  TranscriptionFactor = c(FALSE, FALSE)
)
table |> synStoreRows(values = moreGenes)
## [syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe]: Found 1 chunks to upload into table
## NULL

Updating existing rows

Updating the existing table requires querying the rows you want to change first, since Synapse needs the ROW_ID and ROW_VERSION for each row being modified — synQuery() includes these columns by default. Minimizing changesets to contain only rows that actually change will make processing faster.

For example, let’s update the names of some of our favorite genes:

results = synQuery(sprintf("SELECT * FROM %s WHERE Chromosome = '1'", table$id))
## [syn77792773]: Downloaded to /Users/danlu/.synapseCache/479/177767479/SYNAPSE_TABLE_QUERY_177767479.csv
results$Name = c("rzing", "zing1", "zing2", "zing3")
table |> synStoreRows(values = results)
## [syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe]: Found 1 chunks to upload into table
## NULL

Now, query the table again to see your changes:

synQuery(sprintf("SELECT * FROM %s LIMIT 10", table$id))
## [syn77792773]: Downloaded to /Users/danlu/.synapseCache/481/177767481/SYNAPSE_TABLE_QUERY_177767481.csv
##    ROW_ID ROW_VERSION  Name Chromosome  Start    End Strand TranscriptionFactor
## 1       1           4 rzing          1  12345  12600      +               FALSE
## 2       2           1   arg          2  20001  20200      +               FALSE
## 3       3           1   zap          2  30033  30999      -               FALSE
## 4       4           4 zing1          1  40444  41444      -               FALSE
## 5       5           4 zing2          1  51234  54567      +                TRUE
## 6       6           4 zing3          1  61234  68686      +               FALSE
## 7       7           2  Qux1          4 201001 202001      +               FALSE
## 8       8           2  Qux2          4 203001 204001      +               FALSE
## 9       9           3  Qux3          4 201001 202001      +               FALSE
## 10     10           3  Qux4          4 203001 204001      +               FALSE

Upserting (Update or Insert) rows

If your data has a primary key, you can use the upsert functionality (synUpsertRows) to update existing rows or insert new rows based on this primary key. This way you won’t have to query for the existing data to update your table. This function does not do deletions.

toUpsert = tibble::tibble(
  Name = c("Qux3", "Qux5"),
  Chromosome = c("4", "4"),
  Start = c(201001L, 203001L),
  End = c(202001L, 204001L),
  Strand = c("-", "+"),
  TranscriptionFactor = c(TRUE, FALSE)
)
# Qux3 will be updated, Qux5 will be inserted
table |> synUpsertRows(values = toUpsert, primary_keys = list("Name"))
## [syn77792773]: Downloaded to /Users/danlu/.synapseCache/485/177767485/SYNAPSE_TABLE_QUERY_177767485.csv[syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe]: Found 1 rows to update and 1 rows to insert[syn77792773:My Favorite Genes_from_dataframe]: Found 1 chunks to upload into table
## NULL

5. Deleting Table Rows & Tables

Deleting specific rows — query for the rows you want to delete and call synDeleteRows() on the results:

table |> synDeleteRows(query = sprintf("SELECT * FROM %s WHERE Strand = '+'", table$id))
## [syn77792773]: Downloaded to /Users/danlu/.synapseCache/487/177767487/SYNAPSE_TABLE_QUERY_177767487.csvFound 8 rows to delete for given query: SELECT * FROM syn77792773 WHERE Strand = '+'
##   ROW_ID ROW_VERSION  Name Chromosome  Start    End Strand TranscriptionFactor
## 1      1           4 rzing          1  12345  12600      +               FALSE
## 2      2           1   arg          2  20001  20200      +               FALSE
## 3      5           4 zing2          1  51234  54567      +                TRUE
## 4      6           4 zing3          1  61234  68686      +               FALSE
## 5      7           2  Qux1          4 201001 202001      +               FALSE
## 6      8           2  Qux2          4 203001 204001      +               FALSE
## 7     10           3  Qux4          4 203001 204001      +               FALSE
## 8     11           6  Qux5          4 203001 204001      +               FALSE

Rows can also be deleted based on a data.frame, where the ROW_ID and ROW_VERSION columns specify the rows to be deleted from the table. In this example, rows 2 and 3 are deleted. See this document that describes the expected columns: https://rest-docs.synapse.org/rest/org/sagebionetworks/repo/model/table/Row.html. Note: ROW_VERSION begins at 1 upon row creation and increases by one with every subsequent update.

table |> synDeleteRows(df = data.frame(ROW_ID = c(2L, 3L), ROW_VERSION = c(1L,1L)))

Deleting the whole table deletes the table and all of its rows:

synDelete(table)
## NULL

Working with dates and datetimes

Synapse DATE columns store an exact moment in time, represented as the number of milliseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. Before upload, the client converts the datetime values in your data to that representation, and how a value is converted depends on whether it carries timezone information. The examples below create a small table with a DATE column and walk through the different ways datetime data can be stored and queried.

table = Table(
    name="Sample Collection Dates",
    parent_id=project$id,
    columns=c(
        Column(name="sample_id", column_type="STRING", maximum_size=20),
        Column(name="collected_on", column_type="DATE")
    )
)
table |> synStore()

Storing timezone-aware datetimes (recommended)

A timezone-aware datetime is converted to UTC exactly — the stored value does not depend on the timezone settings of the machine performing the upload or on the date the upload is run. Localizing with a zone name like "America/Los_Angeles" interprets each value using the UTC offset in effect on that value’s own date, so values on either side of a daylight saving switch are both stored correctly.

df <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("S1", "S2"),
  collected_on = as.POSIXct(
    c(
      "2017-02-14 11:23:00", # winter in Los Angeles (PST, UTC-8)
      "2018-10-01 09:30:00" # summer in Los Angeles (PDT, UTC-7)
      ), 
    tz = "America/Los_Angeles"
  )
)

table |> synStoreRows(values = df)

Storing naive datetimes

A naive datetime (one without tzinfo) is assumed to be in the local timezone of the machine at the time of upload, and that single UTC offset is applied to every value in the upload.

naive_df = data.frame(
  sample_id = c("S3"),
  collected_on = as.POSIXct(
    c("2017-02-14 11:23:00")
  )
)

table |> synStoreRows(values=naive_df)

This is convenient when your data and your machine share a timezone and daylight saving period, but any value whose date falls in a different daylight saving period than the upload date is stored shifted by one hour. Here, 2017-02-14 11:23 is a winter (PST, UTC-8) wall-clock time; uploading it from a machine currently on summer time (PDT, UTC-7) stores 18:23 UTC instead of the correct 19:23 UTC. Midnight values deserve extra care: the same one-hour shift can move a naive midnight to 11 PM of the previous day, changing the calendar date the value displays as. To avoid all of this, localize your data first as shown in the previous example.

Storing dates without a time of day

Plain R Date values (as opposed to datetime values like POSIXct) are treated as midnight on that date and converted the same way timezone-naive datetimes are: using the local timezone of the machine at upload time, with the same daylight-saving-shift risk described above.

date_df <- data.frame(
  sample_id = "S4",
  collected_on = as.Date("2017-02-14") # a date, not a datetime
)

table |> synStoreRows(values = date_df)

query_results <- synQuery(
  sprintf("SELECT sample_id, collected_on FROM %s ORDER BY collected_on", table$id),
  convert_to_datetime = TRUE
)
print(query_results)

Loading date columns from a CSV

When storing rows from a CSV file, use date_columns and date_format to tell the client which columns hold formatted date strings and how to parse them. Including the UTC offset in the strings (parsed by %z) keeps the values timezone-aware, with the same benefits as localizing a DataFrame column.

writeLines(
  c(
    "sample_id,collected_on",
    "S5,2017-02-14 11:23 -0800",
    "S6,2018-10-01 09:30 -0700"
  ),
  "collection_dates.csv"
)

table |> synStoreRows(
  values = "collection_dates.csv",
  date_columns = c("collected_on"),
  date_format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %z"
)

Querying datetime data back

By default, querying a table returns DATE columns as raw millisecond timestamps rather than R date/time objects.

Don’t try to reconstruct a date from that raw value yourself. Synapse stores DATE values as 64-bit epoch-millisecond integers, but R has no native 64-bit integer type, and converting a raw integer that large from Python to R isn’t a safe, bounds-checked cast the way as.integer() is — the value can silently wrap around to a different, still plausible-looking integer with no warning that anything went wrong.

Instead, pass convert_to_datetime=TRUE so DATE columns are converted to timezone-aware datetimes in UTC on the Python side:

results <- synQuery(
  sprintf("SELECT * FROM %s ORDER BY collected_on", table$id),
  convert_to_datetime = TRUE
)
results

The collected_on column above may still print as a plain number rather than a date — that’s misleading, not wrong. Each converted value crosses from Python into R individually rather than as one vectorized column, so collected_on comes back as an R list-column: one correct POSIXct object per cell rather than a single date/time vector. R’s default data.frame printing silently drops the class when displaying a list-column, showing the raw epoch-seconds number underneath instead. Flatten it into a normal POSIXct vector with c() before using it:

results$collected_on <- do.call(c, results$collected_on)
results

DATE columns are returned as UTC datetimes. Set the display timezone to view the same instants on another wall clock:

attr(results$collected_on, "tzone") <- "America/Los_Angeles"
results

Note how the timezone-aware rows (S1, S2, S5, S6) round-trip back to the exact wall-clock times they were created with, while the naive datetime row S3 and date row S4 were converted using that same upload-time PDT offset. For S4, that offset is applied to midnight because dates have no time of day.

To filter on a DATE column in a query, compare it against epoch milliseconds:

# In a WHERE clause, compare a DATE column against epoch milliseconds:
# Example: filter for rows where 'collected_on' is on or after January 1, 2018
cutoff <- as.numeric(as.POSIXct("2018-01-01 00:00:00", tz = "UTC")) * 1000 # as double
recent <- synQuery(
  sprintf("SELECT sample_id FROM %s WHERE collected_on >= %.0f", table$id, cutoff),
  include_row_id_and_row_version=FALSE
)
recent

For the full details of how datetime values are interpreted during upload, see the synStoreRows reference documentation.

Clean Up

Delete the project and all its contents when done:

synDelete(project)
